_note: Materials that branch nodes consume and no other file here makes. Each entry states its composition or stoichiometry; heat is a physical floor and labour is borrowed from a named neighbouring entry or left out, and says so.

glass_borosilicate_kg.basis: per tonne of melted and fined borosilicate glass ('metal'), before working into objects
glass_borosilicate_kg.yield_basis: COMPOSITION AND STOICHIOMETRY. Laboratory borosilicate (the 3.3 expansion-class glass) is about 81% SiO2, 13% B2O3, 4% Na2O and 2% Al2O3 by mass. Silica comes as clean quartz sand at its own mass. Boric oxide comes from boric acid: 2 H3BO3 -> B2O3 + 3 H2O, so 2*61.83/69.62 kg of acid per kg of B2O3. Soda comes from natron (Na2CO3.10H2O), 286.14/61.98 kg per kg of Na2O, the alkali source glass_raw_kg uses. The 2% alumina is left out (an impurity carried in with sand and clay); boron volatilised from the melt is not modelled, so both understate the batch slightly. Melting is thermal_mj at the roughly 1500 C this glass needs, taken as the sensible-plus-latent heat of the batch (about 3 GJ per tonne), a physical floor rather than a furnace efficiency; the crew hours are copied from glass_raw_kg's melt because no separate evidence exists for a hotter one. Furnace capital is not modelled here. Heuristic labour and energy, conf C.

glass_lead_kg.basis: per tonne of melted and fined lead crystal (flint glass) metal, before working into objects
glass_lead_kg.yield_basis: COMPOSITION AND STOICHIOMETRY. Lead crystal is roughly 60% SiO2, 30% PbO and the remainder alkali flux by mass. Lead enters as metal and is oxidised in the pot, so the lead needed is 207.2/223.2 kg per kg of PbO. The flux is given as sodium oxide from natron (286.14/61.98 kg per kg Na2O) at about the mole equivalent of the potash that traditional flint glass used, since no potash material exists here. Melting reuses glass_raw_kg's fuel and crew, because a lead glass melts in the same 1000-1300 C range with the same pot furnace; the heat figure is therefore that entry's, not a new one. Heuristic fuel and labour, conf C.

cement_portland_kg.basis: per tonne of ground Portland cement clinker (setting-regulator gypsum not included)
cement_portland_kg.yield_basis: COMPOSITION AND STOICHIOMETRY. Portland clinker is about 65% CaO, with silica, alumina and iron oxide making up most of the rest (roughly 29% together). Lime is supplied as limestone at 100.09/56.08 kg CaCO3 per kg of CaO (CO2 driven off). The oxide balance comes from clay taken as about 87% oxide after dehydroxylation (the same water loss porcelain_kg's kaolinite figure uses). Heat is the enthalpy to calcine and clinker the charge, about 1.75 GJ per tonne, a theoretical floor at the roughly 1450 C clinkering needs; real kilns burn several times more. Crew hours are lime_kg's kiln hours because no cement-specific figure exists here. The few percent of gypsum that retards set is omitted. Heuristic labour and energy, conf C.

stainless_steel_kg.basis: per tonne of austenitic stainless steel (about 18% Cr, 8% Ni, balance iron) cast from its metals
stainless_steel_kg.yield_basis: COMPOSITION. The 18-8 austenitic grade is defined by its chromium and nickel content, so the recipe is that ratio applied to metal already reduced elsewhere, with the 2% melt loss bronze_kg states for a crucible melt. Steel is taken as the iron balance. Melting is thermal_mj at the sensible-plus-latent heat of iron alloy to about 1500 C (about 1.3 GJ per tonne), a floor, and the crew hours are bronze_kg's melt-and-cast hours. Heuristic labour, conf C.

manganin_kg.basis: per tonne of manganin resistance alloy (about 86% Cu, 12% Mn, 2% Ni)
manganin_kg.yield_basis: COMPOSITION. Manganin is defined by its 86/12/2 copper, manganese and nickel ratio, applied to metals reduced elsewhere, with bronze_kg's 2% crucible melt loss. Melting is thermal_mj at the sensible-plus-latent heat of a copper-base alloy to about 1050 C (about 0.6 GJ per tonne), a floor; crew hours are bronze_kg's. Heuristic labour, conf C.

constantan_kg.basis: per tonne of constantan (about 55% Cu, 45% Ni)
constantan_kg.yield_basis: COMPOSITION. Constantan is the copper-nickel alloy near 55/45 by mass, applied to metals reduced elsewhere, with bronze_kg's 2% crucible melt loss. Melting is thermal_mj at the sensible-plus-latent heat of a copper-nickel alloy to about 1300 C (about 0.8 GJ per tonne), a floor; crew hours are bronze_kg's. Heuristic labour, conf C.

nichrome_kg.basis: per tonne of nichrome resistance alloy (about 80% Ni, 20% Cr)
nichrome_kg.yield_basis: COMPOSITION. Nichrome is the 80/20 nickel-chromium alloy, applied to metals reduced elsewhere, with bronze_kg's 2% crucible melt loss. Melting is thermal_mj at the sensible-plus-latent heat of a nickel alloy to about 1450 C (about 0.95 GJ per tonne), a floor; crew hours are bronze_kg's. Heuristic labour, conf C.

type_metal_kg.basis: per tonne of type metal (about 80% Pb, 15% Sb, 5% Sn)
type_metal_kg.yield_basis: COMPOSITION. Printer's type metal is a low-melting lead-antimony-tin alloy near 80/15/5, applied to metals reduced elsewhere, with bronze_kg's 2% crucible melt loss. It melts near 300 C, so thermal_mj is only the sensible-plus-latent heat of a lead alloy to about 400 C (about 0.1 GJ per tonne), a floor; crew hours are bronze_kg's. Heuristic labour, conf C.

zinc_sulfide_kg.basis: per tonne of zinc sulfide made by direct combination of zinc and sulfur
zinc_sulfide_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRY. Zn + S -> ZnS, so 65.38/97.44 kg of zinc and 32.06/97.44 kg of sulfur per kg, assuming complete reaction (the reaction is exothermic and needs no added heat). Labour is not modelled here, a heuristic gap, conf C.

silver_nitrate_kg.basis: per tonne of silver nitrate from silver dissolved in nitric acid
silver_nitrate_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRY. 3 Ag + 4 HNO3 -> 3 AgNO3 + NO + 2 H2O, so per kg of product 107.87/169.87 kg of silver and (4/3)*63.01/169.87 kg of nitric acid (taken as 100% acid), assuming complete reaction. Crystallising and drying labour is not modelled, a heuristic gap, conf C.

capital.good: stoneware dissolving vessels and dark crystallising room
capital.capital_basis: Silver is dissolved in nitric acid in glazed vessels and crystallised out of the light for photography and mirror-silvering; the trade ran to a few tonnes a year at most. Masses are reasoned estimates. Masses and output are the author's estimate (grade D, no opened figure bounds the mass or capacity); no page opened gave silver nitrate plant sizes. Pass 10: still D. Missing: batch size and vessel volumes for silver nitrate, and room size (no opened page).

phosphoric_acid_kg.basis: per tonne of phosphoric acid (H3PO4 content) from bone ash digested in sulfuric acid
phosphoric_acid_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRY. Ca3(PO4)2 + 3 H2SO4 -> 2 H3PO4 + 3 CaSO4, so per kg of H3PO4 310.18/(2*97.99) kg of tricalcium phosphate and 3*98.08/(2*97.99) kg of sulfuric acid (taken as 100% acid). Bone ash is taken as about 75% tricalcium phosphate, a rough composition, so its mass is that stoichiometric figure divided by 0.75. The gypsum by-product is not credited. Labour is a reasoned estimate (conf C): charging bone ash and acid to the digester, settling, decanting and boiling the liquor down comes to about eighty hours a tonne, twenty of them a chemist's.

capital.good: lead-lined digesting vats and evaporating pans
capital.capital_basis: Bone ash is digested in dilute sulphuric acid in wooden vats lined with lead, which resists the acid; the liquor is run off the gypsum and boiled down in lead pans. A works of this size makes about a hundred tonnes of acid a year. Masses are order-of-magnitude figures. Lead lining weight: chestofbooks.com Estimating Sheet Lead Work: 6 lb and 8 lb sheet lead are the weights generally used for lining tanks, 6 lb meaning 6 lb per square foot; 2500 kg is 5500 lb, about 920 square feet of 6 lb lining. Output is the author's estimate (grade D, no opened figure bounds the mass or capacity). Lead labour rate now opened: fixing sheet lead covering is 1.15 to 1.25 m2/h (code 5) and 1.35 to 1.45 m2/h (code 6) for a squad of plumber and mate on flat work (table 'Outputs in m2/hour for fixing lead sheet covering', constructiontechnology2015.blogspot.com/2015/08/roof-coverings-part-03-lead-sheet.html); it is roofing, with no burned or wiped seam time, so it only bounds a lining. Pass 10: still D. Missing: digest batch size and cycle time, hence vat and pan area; output is the author's. PASS 11 (Complaint 671): lead lining labour derived. Roofing squad rate 1.15 to 1.25 m2/h for code 5 lead, squad of plumber and mate (two people, so about 1.7 person-hours per m2); the numbers are in a table image on constructiontechnology2015.blogspot.com (roof-coverings-part-03-lead-sheet), read in Pass 10, the page text does not repeat them. Times a labelled factor of 2 for grinding, tinning and burned seams (Tharr (ed.), NIOSH case study, Applied Occupational and Environmental Hygiene 7(2) 1992, stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/205007, opened: tank lining is those three steps; 16 lead workers on two tanks of about 720 m2 of shell; no duration given, so the factor 2 is an assumption), gives about 3.5 person-hours per m2. Lead per m2 at 6 lb per sq ft is 29.3 kg/m2 (chestofbooks.com Estimating Sheet Lead Work, opened: 6 lb and 8 lb lead are generally used for lining tanks). This row: 2500 kg of lead is 85 m2, at 3.5 h/m2 that is 299 h against the row's 400 h of plumber time, within a factor of 1.5, so the plumber hours are kept. Still unsourced, so the row stays D: digester volume (batch and cycle time), timber 20 m3 and carpenter 150 h, output, life. PASS 12 (Complaint 671), still D. Ure (archive.org/stream/dictionaryofarts00urea/dictionaryofarts00urea_djvu.txt, opened, article Phosphorus): 100 lb of bone ash and 78 lb of acid with twice the weight of bone ash in water, 24 hours of digestion, thinned and settled in tall casks, the liquor boiled down in a lead or copper pan to 37 lb of syrup. So one cwt of bone ash yields 37 lb of syrup acid; 100 t of acid a year needs about 270 t of bone ash a year; the batch size and the number of vats and casks are not given, so the vat and pan areas stay unbounded.

caustic_soda_kg.basis: per tonne of sodium hydroxide (NaOH content) from causticising soda ash with lime
caustic_soda_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRY. Na2CO3 + CaO + H2O -> 2 NaOH + CaCO3, so per kg of NaOH 105.99/80.00 kg of sodium carbonate, 56.08/80.00 kg of quicklime and 18.02/80.00 kg of water, assuming complete conversion. Labour is taken from the neighbouring Leblanc soda entry (soda_leblanc: 150 labourer and 60 furnaceman hours a tonne of soda ash): causticising is its leaching, settling and boiling down without the black-ash roasting, about two fifths of it, so 60 labourer and 30 furnaceman hours; conf C.

capital.good: causticising tanks and iron evaporating pans
capital.capital_basis: Soda ash is boiled with slaked lime in iron or timber tanks, the lye settled and drawn off, and boiled down in cast-iron pans, which corrode within years; a works of this size makes about a hundred tonnes of caustic a year, a reasoned figure for an early soap-maker's supplier. Masses are order-of-magnitude figures. Tank type as for lixiviation in lenntech.com Soda industries (www.lenntech.com/chemistry/soda-industries.htm); masses and output are the author's estimate (grade D, no opened figure bounds the mass or capacity). Plate labour now opened: 5 tons a year per man in boiler assembly (Piggott in oldcopper.org/broseley/journals/15.html), 400 h a tonne at 2000 h a year. Pass 10: still D. Missing: causticising batch size and pan area; Britannica 1911 has cast-iron finishing pots of 10 to 20 tons for caustic liquor but no works output. Britannica 1911 Alkali Manufacture (en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Alkali_Manufacture, opened): black-ash charge of salt-cake generally 3 cwt; caustic finishing-pots hold 10 to 20 tons; Mactear mechanical salt-cake pan 17 ft wide; bleaching chambers left 12 hours or more; no vat, pan or tank sizes for the hand plant. Smith hours per tonne: Piggott, quoted in Broseley Local History Society Journal 15 (oldcopper.org/broseley/journals/15.html, opened): boiler-plate assembly (trimmed, formed, punched, caulked, riveted) ran five tons a year per man employed, 1831 to 1864; at 2000 hours a person-year (sim/unit_conversions.py) that is 400 h/t, a plate-work analogue used for vessel work here. This row: 3000 kg of metal at 400 h/t is 1200 h against the old 200 h, a factor of 6.0, so smith hours are set to 1200. Still unsourced, so the row stays D: causticising tank sizes, pot plate thickness, timber and brick, carpenter and mason hours, life. PASS 12 (Complaint 671), still D but bounded. Lunge, Sulphuric Acid and Alkali, alkali volume (https://archive.org/stream/atheoreticaland09lunggoog/atheoreticaland09lunggoog_djvu.txt, opened, chapter Caustic Soda): causticising is done in horizontal semicylindrical vessels, often old boilers cut in half, 20 to 30 ft long and 6 to 7 ft wide and deep, tank liquor diluted to 16 to 20 deg Tw, lime added unslaked, settling half an hour; lime-mud filter 20 x 10 x 4 ft; boat pans 12 x 8 ft x 3 ft 6 in deep with 2 in of cast iron; finishing pots 7 to 9.5 ft across and 4 to 5.5 ft deep, the usual 9 ft x 6 ft 6 in holding 10 tons of caustic, weighing about 6.5 tons, metal 2 in (small) to 8 in (large) thick in the bottom; a pot lasts at least ten months, up to two years, and turns out 600 to 700 tons of caustic if turned every three months. Cross-checks: 100 t a year of NaOH needs 132.5 t of Na2CO3 (2 x 40.0 / 106), at about 10 percent in 16 to 20 deg Tw liquor about 1,300 m3 of liquor a year, 4 m3 a day over 300 days, so a causticiser of a few m3 (a 25 ft half-boiler holds 11.7 m3, so this is a half-boiler a third that size); iron: a 4 t finishing pot at the 10-ton pot's 0.65 t of iron per t is 2.6 t, a 4 m3 causticiser of 12.7 mm plate about 0.8 t, so with a small pan the sum is about 4.4 t against the row's 3.0 t, within a factor of 2, kept; brickwork for the pot setting about 8,700 bricks against the row's 5,000, within a factor of 2, kept. Life: tonnage view 600 to 700 t at 100 t a year is 6 to 7 years, row's 10 years within a factor of 2, kept. Still unsourced, so the row stays D: the 10 m3 of timber and 60 carpenter hours (Lunge names no timber tank in the caustic plant), and the lime-mud filter and settler material.

gunpowder_kg.basis: per tonne of black powder (75% saltpetre, 15% charcoal, 10% sulfur by mass)
gunpowder_kg.yield_basis: COMPOSITION. Black powder is the classical 75/15/10 mixture of saltpetre, charcoal and sulfur by mass; mixing and corning is a physical blend with no reaction and no mass loss. Labour is a reasoned estimate (conf C): an edge-runner mill takes a charge of some fifty kilograms for a few hours with two hands, and corning, glazing, drying and dusting add about as much again, so about a hundred hours a tonne.

capital.good: water-driven powder mill: edge-runner stones, incorporating house and drying stove
capital.capital_basis: One mill house with a pair of edge-runners incorporates about two hundred kilograms of powder a day, so on the order of sixty tonnes in a working year; the mill is built light of timber so an explosion does little harm and is rebuilt or repaired through the decades. Masses are order-of-magnitude figures. Throughput check: Britannica 1911 (en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclopædia_Britannica/Gunpowder) says incorporation takes about four hours under two heavy iron wheels, so a mill running two charges a day at about 100 kg a charge gives the 200 kg a day, about 60 tonnes a working year at 300 days; the charge size and building masses are the author's estimate (grade D, no opened figure bounds the mass or capacity). Pass 10: still D. Missing: runner stone mass, mill house size and charge. A search result (not an opened page) gave a 50 lb charge per bed, 3 hours for cannon and 5 for rifle powder, and about 100,000 lb a year from one pair of runners (Popular Science Monthly vol 6 page 743); the page returned 401, so it is not a citation. Wikipedia Gunpowder mill (opened): Confederate Powderworks at Augusta produced 6,000 tonnes in 1862 to 1865, scale only; no stone weights, charge or building sizes. Still unsourced, so the row stays D: runner mass, building volumes, labour hours, life.

borax_kg.basis: per tonne of borax decahydrate (Na2B4O7.10H2O) from boric acid and soda
borax_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRY. 4 H3BO3 + Na2CO3 + 5 H2O -> Na2B4O7.10H2O + CO2 (borax decahydrate is 381.37 g/mol), assuming complete reaction. Crystallising labour and heat are not modelled, a heuristic gap, conf C.

capital.capital_basis: Boric acid is dissolved with soda ash in a hot lead-lined pan and the borax crystallised out in tanks; lead resists the alkaline liquor. A refinery of this size turns out about a hundred tonnes a year. Masses are order-of-magnitude figures. Process: Britannica 1911 (en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclopædia_Britannica/Borax) says borax is made by dissolving soda in lead-lined steam-heated pans and adding boric acid; chestofbooks.com Estimating Sheet Lead Work: 6 lb and 8 lb sheet lead are the weights generally used for lining tanks, 6 lb meaning 6 lb per square foot; 1000 kg is 2200 lb, about 370 square feet of 6 lb lining. Output is the author's estimate (grade D, no opened figure bounds the mass or capacity). Lead labour rate now opened: fixing sheet lead covering is 1.15 to 1.25 m2/h (code 5) and 1.35 to 1.45 m2/h (code 6) for a squad of plumber and mate on flat work (table 'Outputs in m2/hour for fixing lead sheet covering', constructiontechnology2015.blogspot.com/2015/08/roof-coverings-part-03-lead-sheet.html); it is roofing, with no burned or wiped seam time, so it only bounds a lining. Pass 10: still D. Missing: borax batch size and crystallising time, hence tank area; output is the author's. PASS 11 (Complaint 671): lead lining labour derived. Roofing squad rate 1.15 to 1.25 m2/h for code 5 lead, squad of plumber and mate (two people, so about 1.7 person-hours per m2); the numbers are in a table image on constructiontechnology2015.blogspot.com (roof-coverings-part-03-lead-sheet), read in Pass 10, the page text does not repeat them. Times a labelled factor of 2 for grinding, tinning and burned seams (Tharr (ed.), NIOSH case study, Applied Occupational and Environmental Hygiene 7(2) 1992, stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/205007, opened: tank lining is those three steps; 16 lead workers on two tanks of about 720 m2 of shell; no duration given, so the factor 2 is an assumption), gives about 3.5 person-hours per m2. Lead per m2 at 6 lb per sq ft is 29.3 kg/m2 (chestofbooks.com Estimating Sheet Lead Work, opened: 6 lb and 8 lb lead are generally used for lining tanks). This row: 1000 kg of lead is 34 m2, at 3.5 h/m2 that is 119 h against the row's 150 h of plumber time, within a factor of 1.5, so the plumber hours are kept. Crystal yield per batch from Wikipedia Borax (opened) solubility table: saturated solution is 44.31 percent borax by mass at 80 C and 4.70 percent at 20 C; with decahydrate 1.895 times the anhydrous mass, cooling 100 kg of hot liquor deposits about 82 kg of decahydrate crystals (44.31 - x/1.895 = 0.047 (100 - x) gives x = 82), so about 1.2 t of liquor per tonne of crystals. Still unsourced, so the row stays D: crystallising cycle time (so number of tanks), timber 8 m3 and carpenter 100 h, output, life. PASS 12 (Complaint 671), conf D to C. Batch and vessel sizes opened: Muspratt, Chemistry Theoretical, Practical and Analytical vol 1, article Borax (https://archive.org/stream/chemistrytheoret01muspuoft/chemistrytheoret01muspuoft_djvu.txt, opened): a batch dissolves 23 cwt of crystallised soda in a lead-lined wooden steam-heated vat to about two tons of liquor, then about one ton of Tuscan boracic acid (nearly 10 percent foreign matter) is added; liquor at specific gravity 1.166 settles 10 to 12 hours and runs to shallow lead-lined crystallising vessels; refining dissolves about nine tons of crude borax and crystallises it in lead-lined wooden vessels 5 to 6 ft deep, 4 ft wide and 20 to 30 ft long, with tight lead-lined lids, for 25 to 30 hours. Derived batch: 1 ton of acid at 90 percent H3BO3 (61.8 g/mol) is 14.7 kmol, 23 cwt soda crystals (286 g/mol) is 4.1 kmol, so about 3.7 kmol of borax decahydrate (381 g/mol) is 1.4 t a batch; 100 t a year (entry output, the plant is sized to it) is about 71 batches a year, one batch every 4 to 5 working days, so one dissolving vat and one refining crystalliser serve with room to spare. Lead area, with every proportion below an assumption of mine: dissolving vat about 1.7 m3 (two tons at 1.166), cylinder 1.2 m across and 1.5 m deep, lined area 6.8 m2; first crystalliser of the same volume, 3.0 x 1.0 x 0.6 m, lined area 7.8 m2; refining crystalliser scaled from Muspratt's 5.5 x 4 x 25 ft (15.6 m3 for 9 t) to a 1.4 t batch, 2.4 m3, 0.65 x 0.9 x 4.1 m, lined area with lid 13.9 m2; total 28.5 m2. At 6 lb or 8 lb per sq ft (chestofbooks.com Estimating Sheet Lead Work, already cited) that is 835 to 1110 kg of lead against the row's 1000 kg, kept. Timber: wooden shells at an assumed 75 mm are 2.1 m3 over 28.5 m2, plus the insulating outer boxes and lids, so the row's 8 m3 is within a factor of 3, kept; carpenter and plumber hours kept (plumber 119 h derived earlier). Life: Lunge, Sulphuric Acid and Alkali (https://archive.org/stream/atheoreticaland02lunggoog/atheoreticaland02lunggoog_djvu.txt, opened) gives 6 lb lead chambers lasting 8 to 10 years on average and up to 20 years at Stolberg; borax liquor is milder than chamber acid, so 15 years is within a factor of 2 of that range. Every figure is now sourced or derived, assumptions labelled, so conf C.
